{{Short description|English chemist}}
'''Peter Jaffrey Wheatley''' (5 March 1921 – 12 May 1997) was an English chemist, who published over 100  papers and 5 books on physical chemistry, crystallography and structural chemistry.

==Biography==

Wheatley was born on 5 March 1921 in Wilmslow, Cheshire. He was educated at [[King Edward VII School (Sheffield)|King Edward VII School]]  ([http://oldedwardians.org.uk/nlc/corporis/cricket1st38-39.html photo]) in [[Sheffield]], where he was Head Prefect in 1938/1940, Captain of cricket for two years and 1st XI footballer for four. He began a degree at Oxford at the start of World War II, but was soon enlisted as a [[Bombardier (rank)|bombardier]]. He was captured during the [[Battle of Singapore|Fall of Singapore]] in 1942. After four years as a prisoner of war, and working on the Burma railway,<ref>{{cite web|title=Transcript of an Interview Conducted by Michael A. Grayson of Raymond E March|website=Chemical Heritage Foundation on behalf of the American Society for Mass Spectrometry|url= https://www.asms.org/docs/default-source/oral-histories/march_re_0921_full.pdf?sfvrsn=2|access-date=29 April 2020}}</ref> and then regaining his health, Wheatley returned to Oxford, studying at [[The Queen's College, Oxford|Queen's College]] (1946-1948) and [[Merton College, Oxford|Merton College]] (1948-1949).<ref name="MCreg">{{cite book|editor1-last=Levens|editor1-first=R.G.C.|title=Merton College Register 1900–1964|date=1964|publisher=Basil Blackwell|location=Oxford|page=386}}</ref> He was awarded a first in chemistry in 1948 and a DPhil in physical chemistry in 1951.<ref name=crystal>{{Cite journal|title= Peter Wheatley (1921 - 1997)|journal=Journal of Applied Crystallography|volume=30|pages=567–68|date=1997}}</ref>

Wheatley married Edna Mary Bolton (known as Jo) in Sheffield in 1948. In September 1949 they sailed First Class from Liverpool on the [[Cunard Line]]’s [[RMS Ascania (1923)|Ascania]] to Quebec, en route to the [[Minneapolis–Saint Paul |Twin Cities]], where Wheatley was a [[Commonwealth Fellow]] at the [[University of Minnesota]] for a year. On their return to the UK the first of their daughters was born in 1950. The following year they moved to Leeds, where Wheatley had a Lectureship in Chemistry. Their two other daughters were born in 1953 and 1954.

Biochemist [[Richard E. Dickerson]] recalls that “in 1957, Peter J. Wheatley despaired of supporting a wife and two children on his Leeds professorial salary of £900 per annum (then $2,500), resigned from the university, and prepared to move to Zurich to head up a new crystallographic unit for [[Monsanto]].”<ref>{{cite journal|last=Dickerson|first=Richard E|title=Recollections: A little ancient history|journal=Protein Science|location=USA|publisher=Cambridge University Press|pages=181–86|date=1992}}</ref>

After nine years in Switzerland, during which time he published several papers,<ref>e.g. {{cite journal|last=Wheatley|first=P J|title=Structure of Lithium Methoxide|journal= Nature|volume=185|pages=681–82|date=1960|issue=4714|doi=10.1038/185681b0|bibcode=1960Natur.185..681W|s2cid=6915735}} ''and'' {{cite journal|last=Wheatley|first=P J|title=The Crystal and Molecular Structure of Pyrimidine|journal=Acta Crystallographica|volume=13|page=80|date=1960|issue=2|doi=10.1107/S0365110X60000200}}</ref> Wheatley spent a year (1966-67) as visiting professor at the Department of Chemistry, [[University of Arizona]], where he published a paper with [[John P. Schaefer]] on the structure of [[anisomycin]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Schaefer|first1=John P|last2=Wheatley|first2=Peter J|title=The Structure of Anisomycin|journal=Chemical Communications|location=London|pages=578–79|date=1967}}</ref>

Wheatley’s last position was in the Department of Physical Chemistry at Cambridge. During his years in Cambridge he became a Fellow of Queens' College “and was renowned at both Departmental and College level for his teaching and lecturing. He also served as British Co-editor of ''Acta Crystallographica'' from 1969 to 1980, processing a phenomenal number of papers with care, knowledge and not a little tact!”<ref name=crystal/> Wheatley was made a Life Fellow of Queens' when he retired in 1988.

Peter Jaffrey Wheatley died on 12 May 1997, aged 76. His ashes were scattered at Cambridge Crematorium four days later.  'Jo' died in Cambridge on 17 July 2005, aged 80; she was cremated on the 29 July.<ref>{{cite web|title=cremation register summary|website=Deceased Online|url=https://www.deceasedonline.com/servlet/GSDOSearch|access-date=30 April 2020}}</ref>

==Publications==
Wheatley published 5 books and more than 100 papers.<ref>{{Cite journal|title= Peter Wheatley (1921 - 1997)|journal=Journal of Applied Crystallography|volume=30|pages=567–68|date=1997}}</ref>
===Books===
* ''Determination of Molecular Structure'', Clarendon Press, Oxford, 1959 (2nd ed, 1981: {{isbn|978-0486640686}})
* ''The Chemical Consequences of Nuclear Spin'', North-Holland Publishing Company, 1970 ({{isbn|978-0720401707}})

===Papers===
A list of 62 papers published from to 1948 to 1981 is shown on the Chemistry Tree website.<ref>{{cite web|title=Peter Jaffrey Wheatley, Ph.D – Publications|website=Chemistry Tree - The Academic Genealogy of Chemistry Researchers|url=https://academictree.org/chemistry/publications.php?pid=72624|access-date=28 April 2020}}</ref>
